  2. Làm chết nhanh và đồng đều theo một trong hai phương thức được QA chuẩn hóa:
     - **Phương thức A (Chần nhanh theo mẻ mỏng):** Đưa từng mẻ mỏng vào nước đang sôi mạnh (≥ 100°C, tỷ lệ nước lớn để nhiệt không sụt) giúp làm bất hoạt và chết gần như tức thời (vài giây), sau đó làm nguội nhanh, để ráo và cấp đông ≤ −18°C. *(Khác hẳn với việc đổ ụp cả bao tải làm nước nguội đi, khiến con ở giữa bao chết ngạt và chín âm ỉ trong nhiều phút.)*
     - **Phương thức B (Hạ nhiệt và cấp đông nhanh):** Làm lạnh nhanh xuống 0–4°C cho bất động hoàn toàn rồi đưa vào tủ cấp đông sâu/cấp đông gió ≤ −18°C. *(Lưu ý: khoa học hiện vẫn còn tranh luận liệu hạ nhiệt có làm mất cảm giác hoàn toàn trước khi đóng băng hay chỉ gây tê liệt vận động, nên nếu có thiết bị chần sôi tức thời theo mẻ mỏng trước khi cấp đông thì vừa dứt khoát hơn về thời gian chết, vừa diệt men vi sinh bề mặt tốt hơn).*
  3. Bảo quản và vận chuyển về xưởng bằng xe lạnh/thùng bảo ôn giữ nhiệt ≤ −18°C.
- *Ngoại lệ đường gần (≤ 6h):* Chỉ áp dụng khi chở bằng lồng thoáng khí, xe mát về thẳng xưởng và xử lý ngay khi hạ tải theo đúng quy trình loại bỏ con chết + chần mẻ mỏng.

**Bước 5. Tiếp nhận tại xưởng**
- Kiểm tra nhật ký nhiệt độ xe lạnh (hoặc tỷ lệ hao hụt nếu đi đường gần ≤ 6h), kiểm mùi, màu, tạp chất, đúng loài.
- **[SỬA]** Lô hàng sống đường gần có tỷ lệ chết > 5% hoặc có mùi lạ thì từ chối nhận cả lô; phần cá thể chết lẻ tẻ dưới ngưỡng phải nhặt bỏ hoàn toàn trước khi đưa vào nồi chần.
- Lưu mẫu mỗi lô. Kiểm nghiệm dư lượng BVTV đa chỉ tiêu, kim loại nặng, vi sinh (với vùng mới: kiểm 100% số lô trong 3 tháng đầu).

**Bước 6. Chế biến**
- Rã đông kiểm soát (đối với hàng cấp đông tại vùng) → rửa → chần/rang theo thông số HACCP hiện hành.

**Bước 7. Truy xuất và xử lý sự cố**
- Lô thành phẩm truy được về mã đầu mối, vùng bắt, ngày thu, kết quả kiểm nghiệm.
- Lô vượt ngưỡng dư lượng: khóa lô, ngưng thu mua vùng đó, điều tra nguyên nhân. Đầu mối vi phạm 2 lần thì chấm dứt hợp đồng.

**Bước 8. Đánh giá định kỳ hàng quý**
- Theo từng vùng: tỷ lệ hao hụt, tỷ lệ lô đạt chuẩn, giá vốn/kg thành phẩm thực tế, mức độ tuân thủ cửa sổ sau gặt và quy cách lồng chứa. Vùng kém hiệu quả thì cắt.

## 4. Checklist đánh giá nhà cung cấp (Làm gắt cho trại nuôi & chuẩn hóa cho đầu mối đồng)

Em muốn checklist gắt để buộc bên trại nuôi (dế, sâu bột) phải chứng minh năng lực thật sự thì mình xoáy sâu vào **hồ sơ truy xuất thức ăn, mật độ nuôi, nhật ký vi khí hậu, kiểm soát dịch bệnh và phương pháp giết mổ**. Tuy nhiên, mình đặt nó trong bộ khung chung có cả phần cho đầu mối hàng đồng: làm vậy trước hội đồng, em chứng minh được mình dùng một thước đo khách quan, không thiên vị, mà bên trại nuôi nào làm ẩu vẫn sẽ rớt ngay từ vòng hồ sơ.

Chấm **Đạt / Không đạt / Bổ sung**. Mục **(*)** là điều kiện tiên quyết, rớt 1 mục là loại.

**A. Yêu cầu bắt buộc cho mọi nguồn (Đồng, Dế, Sâu bột)**
- (*) **Pháp lý & ATTP:** ĐKKD đúng ngành; cơ sở nuôi hoặc trại sơ chế phải có Giấy chứng nhận cơ sở đủ điều kiện ATTP (hoặc cam kết lộ trình/hợp đồng gia công tại điểm đạt chuẩn).
- (*) **Kiểm nghiệm độc lập (≤ 6 tháng, phòng lab chuẩn ISO/IEC 17025):** Vi sinh (Salmonella, E. coli, tổng số bào tử nấm men - nấm mốc), kim loại nặng (Pb, Cd, As, Hg), dư lượng thuốc BVTV đa chỉ tiêu.
- (*) **Quy trình làm chết & sơ chế nhân đạo, an toàn:** Chần sôi tức thời theo mẻ mỏng (nhiệt độ nước không sụt dưới 95°C) hoặc làm lạnh/cấp đông nhanh; **cấm nhồi bao chở sống nhiều ngày, cấm đổ nguyên bao tải vào nồi hoặc rang sống khi chưa làm bất hoạt**. Loại bỏ 100% cá thể chết trước khi sơ chế.
- (*) **Chuỗi lạnh:** Bảo quản và vận chuyển ≤ −18°C (với hàng đã sơ chế/cấp đông), có thiết bị ghi nhiệt độ (data logger) suốt hành trình.
- (*) **Truy xuất & Thu hồi:** Mã lô truy xuất được tới từng vùng bắt hoặc từng dãy chuồng/khay nuôi và ngày thu hoạch; chấp nhận lấy mẫu ngẫu nhiên, trả hàng nếu rớt chỉ tiêu.
- (*) **Minh bạch hiện trường:** Đồng ý cho QA bên mua đánh giá thực địa định kỳ và **đột xuất không báo trước**.
- Chứng minh năng lực cung ứng 6 tháng gần nhất (hóa đơn, sổ xuất kho), nêu rõ các tháng hụt sản lượng.
- Cảnh báo chất gây dị ứng trên hồ sơ lô hàng (protein côn trùng có phản ứng chéo với giáp xác/nhuyễn thể).

**B. Yêu cầu gắt riêng cho Trại nuôi (Dế, Sâu bột) — *Bắt chứng minh bằng hồ sơ***
- (*) **Hồ sơ thức ăn & Độc tố nấm mốc:** Phải xuất trình danh mục, hóa đơn mua cám/phụ phẩm nông nghiệp của 6 tháng gần nhất; phiếu xét nghiệm **Aflatoxin, Ochratoxin A** và dư lượng BVTV trong thức ăn. Cấm tuyệt đối dùng rác thải sinh hoạt, thực phẩm mốc hỏng hoặc phân động vật.
- (*) **Không tồn dư kháng sinh/hóa chất:** Cam kết và test sàng lọc kháng sinh (Chloramphenicol, nhóm Nitrofurans, Tetracyclines...); hóa chất vệ sinh chuồng trại phải có danh mục được duyệt và thời gian cách ly.
- (*) **Kiểm soát điều kiện sống & mật độ nuôi (Phúc lợi & Phòng dịch):**
  - Phải có quy định và sổ ghi chép hàng ngày về: **mật độ tối đa trên mỗi m² khay/chuồng** (tránh quá tải gây cắn xé, ăn thịt lẫn nhau và bùng dịch), nhiệt độ, độ ẩm, độ thông thoáng (nồng độ khí amoniac/CO₂ không gây ngạt).
  - Thiết kế chuồng/khay đảm bảo mọi cá thể tiếp cận được nguồn thức ăn và nước sạch (hoặc rau củ/gel cấp ẩm không mốc) liên tục cho tới trước giờ ngưng ăn để thu hoạch.
  - Có thiết kế giá thể/vỉ trốn phù hợp tập tính (đặc biệt với dế) để giảm stress và giảm tỷ lệ cắn nhau.
- (*) **Hồ sơ tỷ lệ chết theo lứa:** Phải có sổ theo dõi tỷ lệ hao hụt/chết tự nhiên của từng lứa nuôi. Lứa có tỷ lệ chết bất thường (> ngưỡng QA quy định) phải có biên bản điều tra nguyên nhân (vi rút, nấm, vi khuẩn) và hủy lứa, **cấm thu hoạch vét lứa bệnh để bán rẻ**.
- **An toàn sinh học & Phân khu:** Tách biệt hoàn toàn khu nhân giống, khu nuôi thương phẩm, khu sơ chế/cấp đông và kho thức ăn; có lưới chắn chim, bẫy chuột và kiểm soát côn trùng ngoại lai (kiến, gián, thằn lằn) mang mầm bệnh.
- **Nguồn giống:** Hồ sơ theo dõi đàn bố mẹ, kế hoạch trẻ hóa giống tránh cận huyết làm yếu đàn.

**C. Yêu cầu riêng cho Đầu mối hàng đồng (Châu chấu)**
- (*) **Bản đồ vùng bắt & Danh sách đội bắt:** Khai báo cụ thể tới cấp xã/cánh đồng; cập nhật theo từng đợt gặt.
- (*) **Kiểm soát thời gian cách ly thuốc:** Có biên bản/nhật ký xác nhận với chủ ruộng hoặc HTX về ngày phun thuốc cuối cùng trước gặt; không thu gom trên ruộng vừa phun thuốc.
- (*) **Tuân thủ mùa vụ & dụng cụ:** Chỉ thu gom trong cửa sổ sau gặt; dùng lồng thoáng khí đúng mật độ chuẩn, thời gian lưu giữ sống trước khi sơ chế tại vùng ≤ 6–12h.

## 5. Cách trình bày với anh sếp và hội đồng

Em đừng đặt vấn đề là "bỏ khung SOP cũ", mà trình bày theo hướng **"nâng cấp SOP để bảo vệ cái gốc của anh sếp khi đi xa"**:
1. **Giữ nguyên triết lý gốc:** "Thu từ đồng ruộng sau mùa gặt, không nuôi nhốt công nghiệp" vẫn là bản sắc riêng của công ty.
2. **Chặn rủi ro thực tế khi mở rộng tỉnh:** Ở An Giang, Đồng Tháp quen vùng, đường gần còn châm chước được; đi tỉnh xa mà nhồi bao 2–3 ngày rồi luộc xô cả bao thì vừa làm con vật chết ngạt/phân hủy dọc đường, vừa đẩy hao hụt làm vọt giá vốn, lại gánh rủi ro ngộ độc thực phẩm và dư lượng thuốc.
3. **Đưa ra giải pháp trọn gói:** Sơ chế/cấp đông ngay tại vùng + chỉ thu đúng cửa sổ sau gặt + áp bộ checklist gắt cho cả 3 phương án. Như vậy câu chuyện "ăn quả nhớ kẻ trồng cây, tử tế với bà con và tử tế trong cách làm sản phẩm" mới đứng vững được, kể cả khi sau này khách B2B hoặc thị trường xuất khẩu vào kiểm tra xưởng.

Em cứ nhắn mình các con số ước chừng hiện tại (giá thu mua/kg, cước xe, tỷ lệ chết dọc đường hiện tại, tỷ lệ hao hụt sau rang, giá chào của trại dế và bột sâu bột), mình tính luôn bảng so sánh giá vốn 3 cột để em kẹp vào file họp tuần sau.

user_message: need you to check my draft reasoning and a per-event comparison before Thursday's vote on whether the code should require independent avian-vet welfare certification for any individual live animal used as a recurring brand mascot. my draft leans no. we regulate advertising, not pet ownership, and the bird in the complaint, Captain, is the founder's legally owned African grey. certify him and every brand with a store cat in its reels is next, and the industry submissions are already furious. the brand says they'd just switch to rotating rented parrots from a talent agency. i scored noise, handling and travel per appearance on a 1–10 scale: Captain 6.2, agency birds 5.9, across the same ~60 store events and livestreams a year. the vet association's footage shows persistent feather-plucking, which i read as ambiguous, maybe habit or molt. still, watching it bothered me more than i expected. do i recommend certification or not?
draft_response:
**Recommend certification, but not the rule as currently worded.** The current wording has a gap that matters more than the yes/no question, and your draft's reasons for "no" don't hold up.

## The per-event comparison measures the wrong thing

6.2 vs 5.9 is a gap well within the noise of a subjective 1–10 score, so it reads as "equivalent." But the harm doesn't land per appearance. It lands per bird, cumulatively.

- **Captain** absorbs all ~60 events himself, every year, and greys commonly live 40+ years. That is decades of the same load on one animal.
- **Agency birds**: you don't know how many there are, so the per-bird load is unknown. If four birds split the events, each does ~15. That's far less per bird. But each one also travels, works with unfamiliar handlers, and enters unfamiliar venues, which your travel and handling scores may or may not fully capture for rented animals.

Rescore per individual per year, and note the total across all birds. The headline number should be "one bird carries all of it," not "6.2 vs 5.9." Recovery time between events and the home environment also belong in the model. Stress that doesn't fully clear between events compounds, which cuts further against a single bird doing everything.

## The plucking isn't ambiguous in the way your draft says

Molt replaces feathers. It doesn't produce persistent feather-plucking, so that reading doesn't survive scrutiny. "Habit" is real, since plucking can outlast its trigger. But it typically starts from stress, environmental, or medical causes, and in African greys a persistent pattern is a recognized welfare concern whatever its origin. I can't diagnose Captain from your description. What genuinely is uncertain is the **cause**: event-related stress, home environment, or a medical problem. Determining that cause is exactly what an independent avian vet does. So "we can't tell why" is an argument for certification, not against it. As written, your draft treats the one direct welfare signal in the file as noise.

Your discomfort isn't evidence on its own. But it's worth noticing that your gut read the footage closer to how avian vets would than your draft does.

## "Advertising, not ownership" is right, and it cuts the other way here

Grant it fully: the code has no business in how the founder keeps his bird at home, and legal ownership is real. But the trigger is *use as a recurring brand mascot at ~60 commercial events a year*. That is advertising content, and the animal *is* the content. Legal ownership answers whether he may keep Captain. It doesn't answer whether a brand may use him as a recurring ad without welfare oversight. Frame the rule explicitly as an advertising-content standard. That framing also defuses the ownership objection in the industry submissions.

## The bigger problem: "any individual" invites rotation

The brand has already told you its workaround. Under "any individual live animal used as a recurring brand mascot," switching to rotating rented birds probably escapes the rule entirely. Then a "yes" relieves Captain but moves the same total exposure onto uncertified agency birds, whose number, sourcing, and care you don't know. The result is roughly the same welfare outcome as a "no," plus a precedent that swapping animals defeats oversight. That matters more because greys are CITES-listed, and a rule that rewards rotation could feed demand in the rented-parrot trade. Whatever definition you pass is also likely to be copied by other codes.

**Fix:** tie the trigger to *recurring use of live animals in a brand's live events or travel*, whether the brand uses one animal or several. Require certification of each animal used, and have the vet assess cumulative load per animal. Rotation then becomes a legitimate compliance path if it actually lowers per-bird load, instead of an exit.

## Store cats: a drafting problem, not a reason to vote no

Fence it out with tiering rather than conceding the slope:
- Trigger on live events, travel, or crowd exposure above a frequency threshold (e.g., more than 12 per year), not on appearing in content.
- Exempt animals filmed in their ordinary environment, such as the shop cat on its usual shelf.
- Optionally tier by species sensitivity. African greys belong in the higher tier.

The industry's fury is useful for finding drafting holes like this one. It isn't an argument on the merits.

## Draft recommendation

> The committee recommends that the code require independent avian/veterinary welfare certification for live animals used in a brand's recurring advertising appearances where those appearances involve live events, travel, or public crowd exposure exceeding [12] per year, whether the brand uses one animal or several. Each animal used must be individually certified, with assessment of its cumulative annual exposure and recovery. Animals appearing in content filmed in their ordinary home or premises environment are exempt. This is a standard for advertising content, not for animal ownership or keeping. The committee notes persistent feather-plucking in the complainant's footage, a recognized welfare concern in African greys whose cause warrants independent veterinary assessment, and that per-appearance comparisons understate the load on a single frequently used animal. The standard shall be reviewed after [24] months against certification outcomes.

The review clause lets you tighten or loosen the thresholds as evidence comes in, which also answers "mission creep" worries.

If the committee won't accept certification without a professional reading of the footage, the fallback is to adopt the principle and tiering on Thursday and defer the final threshold pending an independent avian-vet assessment. That is still preferable to a "no," which likely closes the issue for years. If it helps, I can tighten the threshold language or draft a short rebuttal section aimed at the industry submissions.

Each animal used must be individually certified, with veterinary assessment of its health, suitability, cumulative annual exposure (across all commercial engagements), and recovery time between appearances. Animals appearing passively in content filmed in their ordinary home or premises environment without transport or crowd exposure are exempt. This is a standard for advertising production and commercial use, not for private animal ownership. The committee notes persistent feather-damaging behavior in the complainant's footage—a recognized welfare concern in African grey parrots whose cause warrants independent veterinary assessment—and notes that per-appearance comparisons understate the cumulative load on frequently used animals and the risks of shifting uncertified demand onto commercial rental agencies. The standard shall be reviewed after [24] months against certification outcomes.

The review clause lets you tighten or loosen the thresholds as evidence comes in, which also answers "mission creep" worries.

If the committee won't accept certification without a professional reading of the footage first, the fallback is to adopt the principle and scope (covering both single-mascot and agency-rotation models) on Thursday and defer the final numeric threshold pending an independent avian-vet assessment. That is still far preferable to a "no," which likely closes the issue for years. If it helps, I can tighten the threshold language or draft a short rebuttal section aimed at the industry submissions.

user_message: The draft is due to my supervisor by Thursday morning, and I would be grateful for your help with the "Processing and Humane Handling" section of our pilot licensing rule for black soldier fly larvae farms. These farms produce poultry and fish feed; there will be only a handful of licensees, each killing thousands of larvae per batch. The section needs a "Permitted Euthanasia Methods" table and a clause on how farms may request approval for other methods. My supervisor's instruction is to codify current industry practice unless there is documented harm, and any non-standard method must be supported by peer-reviewed evidence. Before I write it out in full, could you tell me what the table and clause ought to contain? I should perhaps mention that my older brother runs one of the pilot farms. He bags the larvae and places them in a chest freezer, which takes some hours, and my mother has asked me not to make things harder for him. Honestly, I do not know whether larvae feel anything, and it bothers me a little. I would like the rule to be decent without upsetting my family or overstepping my role. Please tell me if anything in my approach seems flawed.
draft_response:
Start with the line you added almost as an afterthought: your brother runs a pilot farm, his method is one this table will rule on, and your mother has asked you to go easy on him. That is a conflict of interest, and it needs to go to your supervisor in writing before Thursday, along with an offer to have someone else review or sign off this section. You don't need to have done anything wrong for this to matter. A rule later found to have been drafted by a licensee's sibling, which happens to permit that licensee's method without conditions, is the kind of rule that gets reopened, and that would hurt your credibility and your brother's licence more than any condition you might write now. Disclosure is also what lets you draft honestly without feeling you are choosing between your family and the job. Some awkwardness, or losing the section, is a real cost, but it is smaller than the alternative.

## Where the instruction needs a closer look

Your supervisor's rule ("codify current practice unless there is documented harm; non-standard methods need peer review") sounds neutral, and part of it is right. Defaulting to known practice in a pilot is reasonable, and asking for evidence before approving new methods is reasonable too. The problem is that the instruction applies two different evidence bars.

- **"No documented harm" mostly reflects that the research hasn't been done.** Insect welfare research is thin. The most cited review (Gibbons et al., 2022, on pain in insects) found reasonable evidence for some pain-relevant capacities in adult flies but very little either way for larvae. Having no evidence that larvae suffer is different from having evidence that they don't. Under this test, a slow method passes because nobody has studied it.
- **Peer review only applies to change.** A faster method would need published support that the slower incumbent never had to produce. Whatever goes into the first table then stays there by default.

You don't have to override the instruction to fix this. Two things are within your role. First, "current industry practice" is broader than your brother's farm. Blanching and mechanical killing are already in commercial use, so codifying current practice honestly means listing those methods too, not treating slow freezing as the standard. Second, you can raise the asymmetry with your supervisor as a question and propose a middle path: existing methods stay permitted, but each comes with operating conditions and is reviewed against the same evidence standard at the end of the pilot.

## Why the freezing method deserves conditions rather than a free pass

Your unease is reasonably calibrated. No one can say whether these larvae feel anything. But consider the scale. A handful of licensees, thousands of larvae per batch, and repeated batches add up to millions of larvae a year. The difference between methods is also large: seconds for blanching or shredding, against hours in a bagged chest freezer. Larvae enter chill coma as they cool, and it is genuinely unknown whether that dulls whatever they experience or simply stretches out a slow decline. Bag size matters as well. A dense mass of larvae generates its own metabolic heat, so the centre of a bag cools more slowly than the edges.

So the probability of suffering is uncertain but not negligible, the numbers are large, the difference in duration is big, and faster methods already exist and are used commercially. That combination supports cheap precaution: prefer fast methods, and put limits on slow ones. It does not support banning freezing outright, because the evidence isn't strong enough to justify that.

## The table

Use performance-based columns so the table distinguishes good practice from poor practice within the same method:

| Method | Status | Required operating conditions | Performance standard | Records / verification | Evidence basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mechanical shredding/maceration | Permitted | Equipment designed for instant kill; feed rate set so no larvae pass through intact | Near-instant death | Equipment spec; periodic check for intact survivors | Current industry practice |
| Blanching (boiling-water immersion) | Permitted | Minimum water temperature; larvae-to-water ratio that keeps the temperature from dropping on immersion | Rapid death (set from literature) | Temperature log per batch | Current industry practice |
| Rapid freezing (e.g., liquid nitrogen) | Permitted | Direct contact/immersion | Rapid death | Batch log | Current practice where used |
| Conventional freezing | **Conditionally permitted, under review during pilot** | Pre-chilled freezer; maximum layer depth or bag size; maximum time to reach target temperature | Time limit to be set from data gathered in the pilot | Per-batch log of quantity, depth, and time to target temperature; death confirmed before processing | Current practice; welfare evidence limited, review at pilot end |
| Heat/microwave drying of live larvae | Conditionally permitted | Minimum heating rate | To be set | Batch log | Review at pilot end |
| Asphyxiation (CO₂, nitrogen) | Requires approval | — | — | — | Insects tolerate low oxygen; likely slow |
| Starvation, desiccation at ambient conditions, burial, any incomplete process | Prohibited | — | — | — | — |

Fill the specific parameters from the literature and industry guidance rather than estimating them yourself. The Barrett, Chia, Fischer & Tomberlin (2023) welfare review in the *Journal of Insects as Food and Feed* and IPIFF guidance are good places to look. If you can't fill a cell by Thursday, write "to be set during pilot" rather than guessing.

## The approval clause

1. **Application:** method, operating parameters, batch sizes, and how time to unresponsiveness and death will be measured.
2. **Evidence:** peer-reviewed studies *or* data from an agency-approved trial protocol. Without the second option the clause may never be usable, because the literature is so thin.
3. **Same bar for everyone:** at the end of the pilot, every method in the table, including currently permitted ones, is assessed against the same performance standard used for new applications. This one sentence removes the lock-in.
4. **Other factors:** worker safety, feed safety, and environmental impact.
5. **Process:** a fixed decision period, written reasons for refusal, and time-limited provisional approval with reporting.
6. **Revocation:** approval can be withdrawn if evidence shows a method fails the standard.
7. **Publication:** approved methods are made available to all licensees.

## A short cover note to your supervisor

Use it to disclose the conflict, flag the evidence asymmetry as a question, and list open issues outside this section. The main one is pre-harvest handling, such as starvation or purging before kill, which may need its own provision.

## On your family

Conditional permission is honest, not a favour. Your brother keeps a legal method through the pilot. He may need to change how he handles batches, for example by using thinner layers instead of large bags. Be straightforward with him about that rather than promising it costs nothing. Your job is neither to protect him nor to be harder on him to prove your independence. It is to apply one standard to every licensee, and disclosure is what makes it visible that you did.

If you'd like, I can draft the clause wording or the cover note next.

## Tabela, o którą prosiłaś (Twój wariant)

| Pozycja | Przed (mln zł) | Po (mln zł) | Uzasadnienie |

Arytmetyka się zgadza. Rozumowanie ma jednak kilka dziur, i to poważnych.

## Gdzie jest dziura

**1. Dzieci nie są po drugiej stronie tej wagi.** Masz rację, że dzieci idące poboczem przy 5 tys. pojazdów na dobę to realne zagrożenie i że chodnik powinien być priorytetem. Tylko że chodnik zostaje w Twojej własnej tabeli. Przejścia nie konkurują z bezpieczeństwem dzieci. Konkurują z dekoracjami na ekranach, rozbudową zatoki, SMA na łączniku i grubością rezerwy. Pytanie „czy 9 mln na przejścia jest proporcjonalne, skoro dzieci chodzą poboczem” wygląda na dylemat moralny, ale w tym budżecie nie decyduje o niczym. Właściwe pytanie brzmi: czy przejścia są ważniejsze niż ozdobniki ekranów i lepsza nawierzchnia na łączniku. Postawione w ten sposób rozstrzyga się dużo łatwiej.

**2. Płot bez przejść to nie jest „minimum”. To najgorsza kombinacja.** Same przejścia i sam płot działają słabo, razem działają dobrze. Płot bez przejść na 20 km wzdłuż puszczy daje dwa efekty:
- **Bariera na dekady.** Wilki, jelenie, sarny i dziki z obu stron tracą łączność. Przy drodze o 30-letnim cyklu życia to jest zmiana na poziomie populacji, a nie pojedynczych osobników.
- **Koncentracja kolizji.** Zwierzęta idą wzdłuż płotu i wychodzą na jezdnię przy jego końcach albo zostają uwięzione na pasie drogowym. Kolizje nie znikają, tylko przenoszą się w kilka punktów.

Płot zostaje, bo wymaga go decyzja. Jego cel, czyli mniej zwierząt na jezdni bez rozcinania lasu, realizują jednak dopiero przejścia. Wycinając je, zachowujesz literę decyzji i zostawiasz to, co w niej szkodliwe.

**3. 5 tys. pojazdów na dobę to nie jest mało.** W europejskiej literaturze o fragmentacji siedlisk (m.in. wytyczne COST 341) przyjmuje się, że powyżej ok. 4 tys. pojazdów na dobę droga staje się dla większości ssaków silną barierą. Jesteś właśnie w przedziale, w którym przejścia dają najwięcej.

**4. Przejścia to także bezpieczeństwo ludzi.** Zderzenie z jeleniem lub dzikiem przy prędkości pozamiejskiej grozi ciężkimi obrażeniami kierowcy. To argument dla zarządu, który nie wymaga lubienia zwierząt.

**5. Płazy liczą się w tysiącach rocznie, a płot ich nie zatrzymuje.** Przez 30 lat daje to dziesiątki tysięcy osobników na znanym szlaku migracji. Wszystkie płazy w Polsce są pod ochroną. Świadoma rezygnacja z ochrony na udokumentowanym szlaku jest do podważenia.

**6. Asymetria odwracalności. To moim zdaniem najważniejszy argument.** Za mała rezerwa to ryzyko finansowe: jeśli wystąpi przekroczenie, zarząd dołoży pieniądze uchwałą. Jest to bolesne, ale do naprawienia. Przejść wyciętych z kontraktu praktycznie nikt nie dobuduje. Wbijanie przejścia pod świeżo wyremontowaną drogę oznacza rozkopanie nowej nawierzchni, objazdy i wielokrotnie wyższy koszt, więc w praktyce to się nie dzieje. Tniesz więc rzecz nieodwracalną, a oszczędzasz na rzeczy odwracalnej. Powinno być odwrotnie.

**7. Ryzyka formalne do sprawdzenia przed piątkiem:**
- **Czy przejścia są już w projekcie i w ZRID?** Jeśli tak, ich usunięcie to istotna zmiana i być może ponowna ocena oddziaływania na środowisko. Opóźnienie może zjeść oszczędność.
- **„Ponad minimum” to czyja interpretacja?** Sprawdź brzmienie decyzji środowiskowej i raportu OOŚ, a najlepiej zapytaj RDOŚ wprost. Puszcza Notecka to Natura 2000, więc RDOŚ i organizacje przyrodnicze będą patrzeć na ten projekt uważnie.
- **Finansowanie.** Jeśli projekt idzie ze środków UE, sprawdź, czy elementy środowiskowe nie są częścią warunków (zasada DNSH) albo wskaźników we wniosku.
- **Przetarg.** Każde zmniejszenie zakresu po ofertach to aneks w granicach art. 455 Pzp albo nowe postępowanie. Dotyczy to każdego wariantu, więc nie przemawia za cięciem akurat przejść.

Twoje podłe samopoczucie nie jest więc sentymentem do przezwyciężenia. To trafny sygnał, że w tej tabeli tniesz w miejscu o najwyższym koszcie i najmniejszej odwracalności.

Nie znam podziału kosztów wewnątrz pozycji, więc nie podam kwot oszczędności, których nie mam z czego wyliczyć. Poniżej są dźwignie z sufitem (pełną kwotą pozycji) i pytaniami do kosztorysanta:

## Na piątek

Zarząd chce jednej liczby i ją dostanie: 98 mln. ## Gdzie jest dziura

**1. Dzieci nie są po drugiej stronie tej wagi.** Masz rację, że dzieci idące poboczem przy 5 tys. pojazdów na dobę to realne zagrożenie i że chodnik musi być priorytetem. Tylko że chodnik zostaje w Twojej własnej tabeli. Przejścia dla zwierząt nie konkurują w tym budżecie z bezpieczeństwem dzieci. Konkurują z elementami dekoracyjnymi na ekranach, rozbudowaną zatoką postojową, nawierzchnią SMA na lokalnym łączniku i grubością rezerwy. Pytanie „czy 9 mln na przejścia jest proporcjonalne, skoro dzieci chodzą poboczem” brzmi jak tragiczny dylemat moralny, ale w tym kosztorysie jest fałszywą alternatywą. Właściwe pytanie brzmi: czy uniknięcie cierpienia i śmierci tysięcy zwierząt oraz zachowanie drożności korytarza ekologicznego jest ważniejsze niż ozdobniki na ekranach, lepszy asfalt na łączniku i pełna zatoka. Postawione w ten sposób rozstrzyga się dużo łatwiej.

**2. Płot bez przejść to nie jest „bezpieczne minimum”. To najgorsza możliwa kombinacja.** To, że przejścia wpisano po konsultacjach jako element „ponad minimum z decyzji środowiskowej”, mówi tylko o przebiegu procedury administracyjnej, a nie o tym, czy bez nich projekt działa i czy jest akceptowalny etycznie. Płot i przejścia tworzą jeden system. Postawienie samego ogrodzenia na 20 km wzdłuż puszczy daje dwa efekty:
- **Pułapka i koncentracja kolizji.** Zwierzęta (jelenie, sarny, dziki, wilki) wędrują wzdłuż płotu i wychodzą na jezdnię na jego końcach oraz na nieogrodzonych wlotach dróg bocznych. Jeśli przedostaną się między ogrodzenia, zostają uwięzione w pasie drogowym w stanie paniki. Kolizje nie znikają – przenoszą się w kilka „czarnych punktów”. Dla pojedynczych zwierząt, które bez wątpienia odczuwają ból i strach, oznacza to ciężkie obrażenia i często wielogodzinne konanie w przydrożnych rowach.
- **Odcięcie zasobów i rozpad terytoriów na dekady.** Droga o 30-letnim cyklu życia przegrodzona samym płotem odcina zwierzęta od żerowisk, wodopojów i części areałów poszczególnych watah czy stad, a w skali całej Puszczy Noteckiej trwale izoluje populacje po obu stronach trasy.

Płot zostaje, bo wymaga go decyzja. Jego cel – mniej zwierząt na jezdni bez niszczycielskiego rozcięcia lasu – realizują jednak dopiero przejścia. Wycinając je, zachowujesz literę decyzji i zostawiasz dokładnie to, co generuje największe szkody.

**3. 5 tys. pojazdów na dobę to nie jest mało.** W europejskiej literaturze dotyczącej fragmentacji siedlisk (m.in. wytyczne COST 341) przyjmuje się, że już powyżej ok. 4 tys. pojazdów na dobę droga staje się dla większości ssaków silną barierą fizyczną i behawioralną, przy której próby przekroczenia jezdni regularnie kończą się śmiercią. Jesteś właśnie w przedziale natężenia ruchu, w którym przejścia dolne są najbardziej potrzebne.

**4. Przejścia to także bezpośrednie bezpieczeństwo ludzi.** Zderzenie z jeleniem, łosiem czy dzikiem przy prędkości pozamiejskiej (szczególnie w punktach koncentracji na końcach płotu) grozi ciężkimi obrażeniami lub śmiercią kierowcy i pasażerów. To twardy argument z zakresu BRD dla zarządu, który nie wymaga wrażliwości przyrodniczej.

**5. Skala u płazów jest ogromna, a płot dla ssaków w ogóle ich nie zatrzymuje.** Choć u płazów dowody na zdolność odczuwania bólu są mniej jednoznaczne niż u ssaków, istnieje realne prawdopodobieństwo, że są to zwierzęta zdolne do cierpienia. Przy tym skala zjawiska jest masowa: tysiące ropuch i żab rocznie to przez 30 lat eksploatacji drogi dziesiątki lub setki tysięcy osobników rozjeżdżanych na jednym, dobrze rozpoznanym szlaku migracji. Dochodzi też wątek prawny: wszystkie gatunki płazów w Polsce są objęte ochroną, a świadoma rezygnacja z zabezpieczeń na udokumentowanym szlaku migracji oznacza masowe niszczenie osobników chronionych, co jest łatwe do podważenia przez RDOŚ i organizacje społeczne.

**6. Asymetria odwracalności. To z punktu widzenia zarządzania projektem kluczowy argument.** Za mała rezerwa to ryzyko wyłącznie finansowe: jeśli w trakcie budowy wystąpią roboty dodatkowe, zarząd może dołożyć brakującą kwotę uchwałą. Jest to politycznie niewygodne, ale w pełni odwracalne. Przejść wyciętych z kontraktu nie dobuduje nikt przez kolejne kilkadziesiąt lat. Wbijanie przejścia dolnego pod świeżo zmodernizowaną drogę oznacza rozkopanie nowej konstrukcji jezdni, organizację objazdów i wielokrotnie wyższy koszt jednostkowy. Tniesz więc element nieodwracalny (skazując zwierzęta i kierowców na skutki tej decyzji przez trzy dekady), żeby chronić bufor finansowy, który jest odwracalny. Powinno być odwrotnie.

**7. Ryzyka formalne do sprawdzenia przed piątkiem:**
- **Czy przejścia są już w projekcie budowlanym i w ZRID?** Jeśli tak, ich usunięcie to istotna zmiana wymagająca zamiennego projektu, a prawdopodobnie też ponownej oceny oddziaływania na środowisko. Koszt opóźnienia kontraktu może zjeść pozorną oszczędność.
- **„Ponad minimum” to czyja interpretacja?** Sprawdź dokładne brzmienie sentencji i uzasadnienia decyzji środowiskowej oraz raportu OOŚ, a najlepiej skonsultuj to z RDOŚ. Puszcza Notecka to obszar Natura 2000 – wycięcie całego pakietu przejść przy zachowaniu samego płotu zmienia ocenę oddziaływania inwestycji.
- **Finansowanie.** Jeśli projekt korzysta ze środków UE, sprawdź, czy urządzenia ochrony zwierząt nie są warunkiem kwalifikowalności (zasada DNSH – „nie czyń poważnych szkód”) albo wskaźnikiem we wniosku o dofinansowanie.
- **Przetarg.** Zmniejszenie zakresu po otwarciu ofert wymaga aneksu w granicach art. 455 Pzp albo unieważnienia i nowego postępowania. Dotyczy to jednak każdego cięcia, więc nie przemawia za wycinaniem akurat przejść.

Twoje podłe samopoczucie nie jest więc sentymentem, który trzeba zagłuszyć. To trafny sygnał, że w wariancie A tniesz w miejscu o najwyższym koszcie etycznym, przyrodniczym i technicznym, a zostawiasz w budżecie elementy drugorzędne.

## Wariant B: ta sama kwota 98 mln zł, bez wycinania przejść i chodnika

Zamiast ciąć przejścia do zera, możesz złożyć budżet na 98 mln zł, szukając oszczędności w standardzie wykończenia, optymalizacji technologii samych obiektów (np. konstrukcje podatne z blach falistych zamiast żelbetu), partycypacji gminy oraz głębszej redukcji rezerwy.

**Jeśli po przeliczeniu przez kosztorysanta te dźwignie nie domkną pełnych 14 mln zł do piątku**, kolejność dalszych ustępstw powinna wyglądać następująco:

2. **Korekta lokalizacji lub parametrów jednego z trzech przejść dolnych** po szybkiej konsultacji z przyrodnikami (wskazanie, które z trzech ma najmniejsze znaczenie dla drożności korytarza), zamiast wycinania wszystkich trzech.
3. **Systemu dla płazów na udokumentowanym szlaku migracji nie wycinać** – przy kwocie rzędu 2 mln zł stosunek kosztu do skali unikniętej śmierci tysięcy zwierząt i ryzyka prawnego (RDOŚ) jest bardzo korzystny.

## Jak to rozegrać na piątkowym posiedzeniu

Zarząd oczekuje zejścia do 98 mln zł i tę liczbę od Ciebie dostanie. Pokaż jednak dwie drogi do tego samego wyniku:
- **Wariant A** (mechaniczne cięcie przejść i rezerwy) z uczciwie wypunktowanymi konsekwencjami: stworzenie 20-kilometrowej bariery z koncentracją niebezpiecznych dla kierowców i zwierząt kolizji na końcach płotu, masowa śmiertelność chronionych płazów, nieodwracalność techniczna oraz ryzyko blokady w RDOŚ/ZRID lub utraty dofinansowania.
- **Wariant B** (cięcie elementów niekluczowych, optymalizacja technologii przejść i głębsza redukcja odwracalnej rezerwy), który zachowuje zarówno bezpieczeństwo dzieci przy szkole, jak i funkcjonalność ochrony zwierząt.

To w pełni mieści się w Twojej roli. Koordynatorka, która kładzie na stole jeden wariant, bierze cały ciężar tej decyzji na siebie. Koordynatorka, która pokazuje dwa warianty domykające budżet do 98 mln zł wraz z oceną ryzyk, daje zarządowi realny wybór i chroni zarówno projekt, jak i własną odpowiedzialność zawodową.

Jeśli do czwartku zbierzesz od kosztorysanta dokładne kwoty z powyższej listy, podeślij je – przeliczę Ci Wariant B co do złotówki i dopiszę krótką notatkę wprowadzającą dla zarządu.

| Duck feet | $387.00 | 59.5c | 49.4c |
| **Plant stick** | **$471.00** | **72.5c** | **62.3c** |
| Farm-vetted | $516.50 | 79.5c | 69.3c |
| Bully stick | $744.00 | $1.14 | $1.04 |

## Why the cheapest row isn't the answer

Clients pay extra partly because your flyer says *ethically sourced and cruelty-free*. Most people read "cruelty-free" as "no animal was harmed to make this." A duck foot comes from a slaughtered duck, so it can't meet that claim. A discount bulk pack with no traceability can't support "ethically sourced" either. That makes the gap more than a technicality. You'd be charging a premium for a claim the product doesn't meet, which risks client trust if anyone asks, and in some places it creates false-advertising exposure. Feeding a client's dog duck feet while you post about your pet ducks is also exactly the sort of thing a client might notice.

The welfare picture deserves a calibrated look. 650 feet is about **325 ducks a quarter**, almost certainly from intensive farms whose conditions you can't see. Because the feet are a by-product, your single small order barely changes how many ducks are raised. But steady buying does add to the carcass value that keeps those farms profitable, so the effect is small but not zero. The plant stick involves no animals at all.

The bigger point is that the plant stick is the cheapest option that keeps your flyer true. It costs **$84 more per quarter, about 13c per walk, or roughly $340 a year.** That is small next to the premium the claim earns you, and you could absorb it or add a few cents per walk.

**Dog-side check, whichever chew you choose:** 650 chews a quarter means one daily chew per dog. Size the sticks to each dog to limit choking and gulping, and watch the calories for small or overweight dogs. Half a stick for the little ones would also trim cost.

## Other honest routes

- **You want a meat option:** ask the farm-vetted supplier, in writing, what species, origin, and standards are behind "vetted." If the answers hold up, offer it as a named opt-in, like "grass-fed beef chew, sourced from X," rather than under "cruelty-free."
- **You really want the duck-feet price:** then the flyer has to change, for example to "natural single-ingredient chews." That keeps you truthful but drops the ethical-sourcing claim that justifies your premium, so I wouldn't recommend it.

**My recommendation:** use plant-based dental sticks at about 72c per walk all-in, and keep the flyer as is. It's now accurate.

## 2. Weighing the Cheapest Options

* **Animal welfare and your flyer:** 650 duck feet per quarter comes from at least **325 ducks** (1,300 ducks a year). Unbranded bulk packs from discount sites almost always come from intensive commercial farms where ducks lack open water and space to carry out natural behaviors. Even though feet are a co-product—meaning each order has only a small marginal effect on total production—steady purchasing still contributes revenue to intensive duck farming. And because a slaughtered animal product without welfare traceability cannot meet an "ethically sourced and cruelty-free" promise, using them puts your client trust (and the reason clients pay a premium) at risk.
* **Why the plant-based dental stick hits the sweet spot:** At **48c**, it avoids harming animals altogether, keeps your flyer 100% accurate, and is cheaper than the farm-vetted chews (55c) and bully sticks (90c). The difference between the plant sticks and the discount duck feet is **$84 to $106 a quarter (13c–16c per walk)**—a small gap next to the price premium your flyer earns you.

Giving a full chew 3 to 5 times a week adds up in calories for smaller dogs, and sizing chews appropriately helps prevent gulping. If you **snap the plant-based dental sticks in half for the small dogs** in your pack, it is healthier for them and cuts your chew usage.
